spans.content: The molecular evidence of Babesia microti infection
in small mammals collected in Slovenia
D. DUH1 , M. PETROVEC1 , T. TRILAR2 and T. AVSIC-ZUPANC1 *
1 Institute of Microbiology and Immunology, Medical Faculty, 1000 Ljubljana, Slovenia
2 Slovenian Museum of Natural History, 1000 Ljubljana, Slovenia
(Received 10 July 2002; revised 7 October 2002; accepted 7 October 2002)
SUMMARY
In Europe, the zoonotic cycle of Babesia microti has not been determined so far. Recently, B. microti was detected in Ixodes
ricinus ticks in Slovenia by using molecular methods. In order to investigate the mammalian hosts of
B
. microti in Slovenia
we collected 261 small mammals representing 11 species. They were tested for the presence of babesial parasites with a PCR
assay based on the nuclear small subunit rRNA gene (nss-rDNA). The bank vole (Clethrionomys glareolus) and yellow-
necked mouse (Apodemus flavicollis) were infected with
B
. microti. The prevalence rate was
for C. glareolus and
for A. flavicollis. Nucleotide sequences of amplified portions of
B
. microti nss-rDNA from C. glareolus and
A
. flavicollis were
indistinguishable from each other and identical with those previously described in I. ricinus ticks collected in Slovenia. The
results of this study represent molecular evidence of
B
. microti in small mammals in Europe.
Key words: Babesia microti, Clethrionomys glareolus, Apodemus flavicollis, molecular analysis, Slovenia.
INTRODUCTION
Protozoa of the genus Babesia are some of the most
ubiquitous and widespread blood parasites (Telford
et al. 1993). Babesia microti is the main causative
agent of human babesiosis, a tick-borne zoonosis in-
creasingly recognized in the north-eastern and mid-
western USA (Homer et al. 2000 ; Kjemtrup &
Conrad, 2000). The life-cycle of B. microti in the
USA has been well described: the white-footed
mouse (Peromyscus leucopus) is the most important
reservoir and the tick Ixodes scapularis is the main
vector (Piesman & Spielman, 1980; Spielman et al.
1981; Telford & Spielman, 1993). Microtus penn-
sylvanicus, M. montanus and M. ochrogaster serve as
minor reservoir hosts (Watkins et al. 1991; Burkot
However, the zoonotic status of
B
. microti in
Europe remains an open question. In different
countries across Europe this parasite has been found
in a variety of small mammals. The absence of in-
digenous cases of babesiosis caused by B. microti was
explained by the selective feeding behaviour of the
proposed vector I. trianguliceps (Kjemtrup & Con-
rad, 2000). Although I. trianguliceps was experimen-
tally established as a competent vector of B. microti,
this tick species does not bite humans (Randolph,
1995). Recently, B. microti has been detected in
I. ricinus in Slovenia, Poland and Switzerland by
means of molecular identification (Duh, Petrovec &

Avsic-Zupanc, 2001; Skotarczak & Cichocka, 2001;
Foppa et al. 2002). In transmission studies Gray et al.
(2002) demonstrated that I. ricinus could serve as
a vector of
B
. microti in Europe. I. ricinus is defined
as an opportunistic tick species utilizing a wide range
of vertebrates as hosts and it readily bites humans
(Sonenshine, 1993).
In Slovenia, the reservoir of
B
. microti had not
been investigated. Therefore we conducted this study
to determine whether small mammals, captured in
Slovenia, are infected with babesial parasites and also
to assess the DNA sequence homologies between
amplicons derived from small mammals and those
previously obtained from I. ricinus ticks.
MATERIALS AND METHODS
Field collections
Small mammals were trapped between 1996 and 2000
in 2 ecologically different regions of Slovenia: the
Subpannonian (UTM: WM77, WM88, WM96,
XM08, XM09) and the Pre-alpine (UTM: VM41,
VM51, VL49, VL58) region. The vegetation in these
regions comprises predominantly broad-leaved for-
est, coniferous forest of boreal type and elements of
the mountainous Mediterranean (Mrsic, 1997). Ani-
mals were captured in live traps, Eliot special and
Sherman type, and sacrificed by ether hyperanaes-
thesia. To aid identification, animals were weighed
and total head–body length, tail, ear and hind-foot
lengths were measured. The blood was collected from
the axillar artery and thin blood smears were im-
mediately prepared.

Analysis of DNA sequences
DNA was extracted from a small piece
( 1 ~ \mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 } )
) of
spleen from individual animals using the QIAamp
DNA Tissue Kit (Qiagen, GmbH, Hilden, Ger-
many). Homogenized samples were lysed by over-
night incubation at
5 6 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }
in the lysis buffer. Samples
were applied to the QIAamp spin column following
the manufacturer’s instructions.
To detect babesial parasites, each sample was tes-
ted with primers PIRO-A and PIRO-B, which were
designed to amplify the 407, 408 and 435 basepair (bp)
fragments of the nuclear small subunit ribosomal
RNA gene (nss-rDNA) of
B
. odocoilei, B. divergens
and B. microti, respectively (Olmeda et al. 1997 ; Arm-
strong et al. 1998). All samples that demonstrated
a positive reaction with the PIRO-A and -B primer
set were additionally tested with BAB-1 and BAB-4
primers, specific for nss-rDNA of
B
. microti (Persing
et al. 1992). When using primers PIRO-A and -B, the
amplification protocol was slightly changed from the
original description; the annealing temperature was
raised to
6 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }
Distinctive amplicons were sequenced on both
strands by using the BigDye Terminator Cycle Se-
quencing Ready Reaction Kit (ABI PRISM, PE Ap-
plied Biosystems, California, USA). The sequences
obtained were analysed with computer programs
SeqMan and EditSeq of the Lasergene 1999 software
package (Dnastar, Madison, Winsconsin, USA). Se-
quence alignments were performed with the MegA-
lign program of the same software package.

RESULTS
A total of 261 small mammals comprising 11 species
(Table 1) were captured and tested for the presence of
babesial parasites. Only
C
. glareolus and
A
. flavicollis
were infected with babesiae as detected by PCR
(Table 1).
Thin blood smears were not available for all 261
animals tested. However, all animals with positive
blood smears were also positive when tested with
PCR. Intra-erythrocytic parasites of infected animals
displayed various morphologies, mostly small dot
and ring forms, which were centrally placed. When
the erythrocytes were multiply infected, the parasites
were placed on the periphery of the cells (Fig. 1). The
characteristic Maltese cross (tetrad) was rarely seen.
We also noticed that all animals tested positive with
PCR had 8–10 times larger spleen than normally
present in mice.

DISCUSSION
The zoonotic cycle of
B
. microti and its role as an
aetiological agent of human babesiosis in the USA is
well known (Kjemtrup & Conrad, 2000). In Europe,
detection of
B
. microti has been made in a variety of
small mammals by microscopical identification in
Giemsa’s-stained blood smears and by xenodiag-
nosis. The following 10 species proved to be infected:
C. glareolus, Microtus arvalis, M. agrestis, M. socialis,
M. nivalis, Neomys anomalus, A. flavicollis, A.
agrarius, A. sylvaticus and Mus musculus (Sebek,
Rosicky & Sixl, 1977; Walter & Liebisch, 1980;
Healing, 1981; Karbowiak et al. 1999). The preva-
lence rates for
B
. microti vary between
and
depending on the species and numbers of rodents
tested, localities and time of the year (Sebek et al.
1977). However, microscopy is labour-intensive and
requires well-trained microscopists for accurate
identification. Tsuji et al. (2001) has demonstrated
the use of molecular methods in the case of emerging
parasitic infections. They have detected
B
. microti in
rodents in Japan, and the parasites were morpho-
logically identical to the American strain of
B
. microti
but different from the American strain when se-
quences of nss-rDNA were compared (Tsuji et al.
In our study, B. microti has been detected for the
first time in
C
. glareolus and A. flavicollis by PCR and
subsequent sequence analysis. Although,
A
. sylva-
ticus and
A
. agrarius were previously implied as hosts
of
B
. microti in Europe, no babesial parasites were
detected in these 2 animal species collected in Slo-
venia. In our country,
A
. agrarius is found only in
3 isolated locations and it does not share the same
habitat as
A
. flavicollis and C. glareolus. However, A.
sylvaticus is as widely distributed as
A
. flavicollis and
C. glareolus but it prefers an open habitat, meadows
and fields, and it usually harbours less ticks (Krys-
tufek, 1991). The low number of animals per species
could be the reason that none of the remaining 7
species were positive. The prevalence rate for
B
microti determined in our study was
for
C
glareolus and
for
A
. flavicollis. The prevalence
rate is higher than in most European countries prob-
ably due to the greater sensitivity and specificity of
the molecular methods used (Krause et al. 1996).
Parasite morphology was, in many cases, similar to
the other findings in Europe, yet in some animals the
parasites were placed on the periphery of the multiply
infected erythrocytes. In a recent study, Gray et al.
(2002) noticed different morphology in the American
and European strain of B. microti in infected gerbil
erythrocytes. However, the 238 bp long nucleotide
sequences of the nss-rDNA of both strains were
identical (Gray et al. 2002). Small mammals which
tested positive for
B
. microti had dramatically en-
larged spleens. Similar observations have been
B. microti infection in small mammals in Slovenia
previously described and splenomegaly was indicated
as a characteristic feature of
B
. microti-infected ani-
mals (Watkins et al. 1991). Males were more often
infected then females. This is in concordance with
other studies and it is ascribed to the greater activity,
home range size and high testosterone levels of sex-
ually mature males (Hughes & Randolph, 2001).
The nss-rDNA sequences of
B
. microti from
C
glareolus and A. flavicollis were indistinguishable
from each other. Moreover, they were identical
with sequences of nss-rDNA of
B
. microti obtained
from I. ricinus ticks, collected in the same zoogeo-
graphical regions in Slovenia (Duh et al. 2001). The
German strain of
B
. microti, isolated from I. ricinus
nymphs in Berlin in 1982, was recently sequenced
(Zahler, Rinder & Gothe, 2000). When compared,
the sequence of
B
. microti strain from Germany
(AF231349) showed
identity with the se-
quences of nss-rDNA of
B
. microti obtained from
small mammals and from ticks in Slovenia. Only 1
nucleotide difference (G–A, transition mutation) was
seen when the above-mentioned sequences were
compared to the American strain of
B
. microti
The puzzling question of the absence of indigenous
human cases of babesiosis caused by
B
. microti in
Europe, remains to be answered. The molecular
characterization of
B
. microti in small mammals as
well as in ticks in Slovenia clearly indicates the wide
distribution of this parasite in nature. In Japan, B.
microti-like parasites were detected in rodents. How-
ever, only 1 transfusion-acquired case of human ba-
besiosis has been described so far (Tsuji et al. 2001 ;
Wei et al. 2001). They suggested that
B
. microti in the
USA may be more pathogenic and virulent for hu-
mans. Further implication of a lower virulence of the
European strain of B. microti was recently presented
by Foppa et al. (2002) in Switzerland. The results
of their study indicated that residents in Switzerland
are exposed to bites of I. ricinus ticks infected with
B. microti. Namely,
of human sera were im-
munoglobulin G-reactive against
B
. microti antigen
yet no clinically documented cases of human babe-
siosis were described (Foppa et al. 2002).
In conclusion, our results represent the first study
in Europe, in which
B
. microti has been directly
identified in C. glareolus and A. flavicollis by PCR and
subsequent sequence analysis.
